B15_00: The Golgi apparatus is dismantled during mitosis so its membranes can be partitioned between daughter cells. Cyclin-dependent kinase 1 together with polo-like and VRK kinases phosphorylate golgins, a Golgi SNARE and an Arf guanine-nucleotide exchange factor, severing golgin-mediated tethering between cisternae and suspending vesicle fusion. Stacked ribbon is thereby converted into dispersed tubules and vesicles, and fragmentation is monitored as a mitotic entry checkpoint.
B15_01: A mature multilayered myelin sheath is actively maintained so it stays intact and compacted. A PDZ-domain scaffold anchors the outer sheath membrane to the basal lamina through a dystroglycan complex, adaptor and NDRG-family proteins handle membrane trafficking and turnover, plectin provides cytoskeletal linkage, and a fatty acid 2-hydroxylase supplies hydroxylated sphingolipids that stabilise the sheath, while Akt signalling sustains continual renewal.
B15_02: The compactness, position and connectivity of stacked Golgi cisternae are actively set and reset. A-kinase anchoring and related scaffolds nucleate and anchor microtubules at the Golgi, CAMSAP proteins stabilise minus ends of these arrays, and a myosin V motor supports actin-based positioning. Rab GTPases direct intra-Golgi and retrograde traffic, syntaxins execute fusion that keeps cisternae continuous, and ERK signalling severs the ribbon at mitosis.
B15_03: Phosphatidylserine, normally confined to the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane, is exposed on the outer surface when lipid asymmetry collapses during apoptosis. A caspase-cleaved XK-related scramblase and other phospholipid scramblases move the anionic lipid outward, where bridging molecules and receptors recognise it as an engulfment signal. Death-receptor ligand signalling initiates the process, and calcium-driven scrambling can cause comparable exposure.
B15_04: Cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich plasma membrane microdomains are assembled to concentrate receptors, channels and signalling enzymes. Caveolins oligomerise in the membrane to drive invagination of caveolae, flotillins mark a separate raft population, and an F-BAR protein bends membrane and couples it to the cytoskeleton. Integrin-linked kinase, an IQGAP scaffold and matrix contacts tie domain organisation to actin and adhesion.
B15_05: A sealed nuclear envelope is rebuilt around decondensing chromosomes after mitosis. An ESCRT-III machine seals holes: one subunit recruits CHMP4 and partners to the reforming envelope, and VPS4 ATPases recycle them once gaps close. Reticulon-like REEP proteins keep ER tubules away from chromatin, spastin severs residual spindle microtubules, BAF with its regulator tethers membranes to chromatin, and RCC1 restores the Ran gradient for transport.
B15_06: The nuclear envelope is disassembled in mitosis and rebuilt around each daughter genome. Barrier-to-autointegration factor tethers chromatin to inner membrane proteins, its phosphorylation cycle controlled by an ankyrin-repeat regulator; ESCRT-associated activities seal final gaps, spastin clears trapped spindle microtubules, and REEP proteins clear ER from chromatin. SUMO conjugation and RCC1-generated Ran-GTP gradients coordinate these events in space and time.
B15_07: Stacked, functional Golgi cisternae are reformed from mitotic fragments, enabling organelle inheritance. Membrane fusion is central: a deubiquitinating enzyme acting on p97/VCP-associated substrates removes ubiquitin marks that keep mitotic membranes apart. A 14-3-3 adaptor and a CCM3-STK25 kinase module link Golgi architecture to polarity and stress signalling, and a Golgi lipid-transfer protein supports organelle organisation.
B15_08: Proteins with a single C-terminal transmembrane anchor are inserted into the ER membrane after translation is complete. A cytosolic pretargeting complex built around BAG6, a co-chaperone and GET4 shields the hydrophobic tail and loads it onto the GET3 ATPase, which docks at a GET1-CAML receptor for release into the bilayer. The EMC complex provides a parallel insertase, and failed substrates are routed to ubiquitin-dependent degradation.
B15_09: Multi-pass membrane proteins have their transmembrane helices threaded into the ER bilayer with correct orientation and topology. After the SEC61 channel delivers the first segments, a dedicated multi-pass translocon takes over, integrating remaining helices while holding them in a protected lipid environment until they pack together. Its components include a TMCO1-CCDC47 module and a nicalin-NOMO-TMEM147 assembly with associated small ER proteins.
B15_10: Endosomes are shaped, matured and positioned so internalised material reaches lysosomes, recycles to the surface or enters autophagic membranes. A small GTPase marking late endosomes licenses lysosome fusion, a lysosomal membrane protein delivers a glucocerebrosidase, a phosphoinositide phosphatase controls lipid identity during uncoating, an adaptor engages ubiquitinated cargo and autophagic machinery, and a ubiquitin ligase supports damaged-organelle clearance.
B15_11: A polygonal network of narrow ER tubules is built and maintained. Reticulons and related hairpin-containing proteins wedge into one membrane leaflet to impose high curvature and stabilise tubules and sheet edges, while atlastin GTPases catalyse homotypic fusion between tubule tips to form three-way junctions that make the network continuous. Tubules host contacts with other organelles for lipid transfer and calcium exchange.
B15_12: Surface membrane invaginates as a network of transverse tubules that carry depolarization deep into the cell, coupling excitation to calcium release and contraction. A BAR-domain protein generates and stabilises tubular invaginations, a caveolin supplies caveolae at tubule openings, and an ankyrin targets channels to the correct domain. A SERCA pump and a tubular membrane protein tie the structure to calcium handling, and a LIM protein links it to mechanosensing.
B15_13: Transport vesicles fuse with Golgi cisternae to deliver cargo. Long coiled-coil tethers first capture incoming vesicles at a distance and hold them against the Golgi membrane, then SNARE proteins on the two bilayers zipper into a four-helix bundle that forces lipid mixing. Different SNARE sets serve ER-derived arrivals at cis-Golgi and endosomal arrivals at trans-Golgi, and Yip-family membrane proteins support Golgi organisation and ER exit sites.
B15_14: Rising cytosolic calcium activates scramblases that let phosphatidylcholine and other phospholipids flip between leaflets, collapsing plasma membrane lipid asymmetry. Anoctamin-family proteins act as calcium-dependent phospholipid scramblases, and a phospholipid scramblase family member adds further calcium-responsive movement. The activity exposes phosphatidylserine on the surface, providing a procoagulant platform, an engulfment signal and a driver of microvesicle shedding.
B15_15: An insoluble protein-lipid shell is assembled beneath the plasma membrane during terminal differentiation. Structural proteins are crosslinked under the membrane while lipid precursors are delivered by secretion of lamellar bodies and processed into sealing lamellar sheets. A MAF-family transcription factor and a histone deacetylase control the differentiation programme, syntaxin-family SNAREs support secretion, glucosylceramide synthesis supplies lipids, and a secreted protein contributes.
B15_16: The ER network is positioned and tethered to the plasma membrane and other organelles to form membrane contact sites. Extended synaptotagmins tether cortical ER in a calcium- and lipid-regulated manner and transfer glycerolipids across the gap, a GRAM-domain protein marks a separate class of contacts, and VAP proteins capture FFAT-motif partners, building contacts for sterol and phosphoinositide transfer and refilling ER calcium stores.
B15_17: Endosomal membrane is deformed into tubular extensions that concentrate cargo and are pinched off as recycling carriers. BAR-domain sorting nexins form heterodimers that sense curvature, scaffold tubules and select cargo, and an ER-resident protein acts at contact sites where tubules are constricted and severed. A coronin actin regulator and a MICAL-family Rab effector tie tubule formation to the cytoskeleton and to recycling routes.
B15_18: A stop-transfer sequence halts translocation into the ER and becomes a stable membrane-spanning helix, establishing membrane protein topology. Subunits of the ER membrane protein complex form a multisubunit insertase working alongside the main translocon, providing a hydrophilic vestibule that lowers the energetic cost of inserting weakly hydrophobic segments and acting as a chaperone for their assembly; failed clients are degraded.
B15_19: The nuclear envelope is broken down so that spindle microtubules can reach chromosomes. CDK1-cyclin, Polo-like, NEK and VRK kinases and protein kinase C phosphorylate lamins, nuclear pore components and inner membrane proteins, dissolving the lamina and chromatin-envelope tethers. Dynein with dynactin tears the envelope along microtubules, and a phosphatase regulator activating lipin phosphatidate phosphatase links breakdown to membrane lipid synthesis.
B15_20: A mature myelin sheath is continuously renewed through lipid supply, membrane turnover and transcriptional upkeep after wrapping is complete. A fatty acid 2-hydroxylase supplies hydroxylated sphingolipids, a sheath-specific transcription factor sustains expression of structural sheath genes, a lipid phosphatase restraining PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling sets sheath thickness, and a secreted chaperone contributes extracellular lipid handling.
B15_21: The amount, curvature and junction structure of the tubular ER network are regulated. Reticulon-like and hairpin membrane proteins tune the propensity of the membrane to bend, a lunapark protein stabilises the three-way junctions that keep the network polygonal, and a Rab3 GAP complex links tubular organisation to Rab-dependent regulation, influencing organelle contacts and distribution of lipids and calcium.
B15_22: The production rate of integrin heterodimers, transmembrane receptors linking cells to extracellular matrix, is regulated upstream. A TGF-beta family ligand drives a matrix-adhesion transcriptional programme, a fibrillar collagen chain provides the ligand integrins bind, a NADPH oxidase generates reactive oxygen species for redox-sensitive signalling, and a nuclear hormone receptor adds hormone-dependent transcriptional control, altering adhesion and motility.
B15_23: Individual Golgi stacks are laterally linked into a single continuous ribbon near the centrosome. Golgins and GRASP-family tethers bridge adjacent cisternal rims, a GOLPH3-myosin XVIII complex applies tension that flattens and stretches membranes, and a v-SNARE and a p24-family cargo receptor contribute fusion and cargo functions. The ribbon supports orderly traffic, uniform glycosylation and polarised secretion, and is dismantled at mitosis.
B15_24: Patches of the late endosome limiting membrane bud inward to form intralumenal vesicles that capture ubiquitinated membrane proteins for lysosomal degradation or exosome release. ESCRT complexes act in sequence: ESCRT-0 recognises ubiquitinated cargo, ESCRT-I and ESCRT-II follow, and ESCRT-III CHMP proteins polymerise to constrict and sever the bud neck. The VPS4 AAA-ATPase with VTA1 disassembles the filaments for reuse.
B15_25: The ease and extent of membrane tubulation is controlled, deciding whether a bud constricts and pinches off or a tubular carrier persists. A BAR-domain protein senses and imposes curvature, a dynamin-like GTPase assembles collars around tubular necks and drives fission, an ARF GAP couples membrane shaping to cytoskeletal and adhesion signalling, a nucleation-promoting factor recruits actin polymerisation, and a flippase alters lipid asymmetry.
B15_26: Plasma membrane tears are resealed within seconds, triggered by calcium entering through the lesion. An annexin with its S100 partner binds calcium and phospholipid and nucleates repair, a giant scaffold organises the submembrane complex, non-muscle myosin II draws wound edges together, and a Rab GTPase with a synaptotagmin-like effector directs vesicles to patch the surface. Caspase-7 links unrepairable damage to apoptosis.
B15_27: A branching network of narrow, highly curved ER tubules is formed. Reticulon-family and related hairpin proteins insert wedge-like hydrophobic domains into the bilayer to generate and stabilise high curvature, restricting themselves to tubules and sheet edges, while protrudin links ER membrane to microtubule-based extension of new tubules. These tubules host contacts with other organelles for lipid transfer and calcium handling.
B15_28: ER tubules are joined by homotypic membrane fusion wherever they meet, keeping the network continuous so lumenal contents, calcium and new proteins can diffuse throughout. Atlastin GTPases tether apposed tubule tips and merge their bilayers through GTP-dependent conformational change, while a SNARE-associated factor and a deubiquitinating enzyme contribute to membrane joining and its regulation, allowing remodelling during growth and after division.
B15_29: Protons are pumped into the endosomal lumen to acidify maturing endosomes, releasing ligands from receptors, freeing iron from transferrin and activating hydrolases. The vacuolar H+-ATPase does this work, with membrane V0 subunits forming the proton channel and cytosolic V1 subunits hydrolysing ATP, assisted by accessory assembly and targeting factors. A chloride transporter provides counterion conductance so the pump does not stall.
